who: A mid-sized farm dog kept mostly for company.
place: The yard outside a small house at dusk, just as its owner comes back on foot after being away most of the day.
present: the returning owner, tired and quiet
a second, older dog lying near the door that barely lifts its head
a chicken pecking near the gate

factors.fact: The dog has lived with this owner for years and treats them as its anchor.
The owner is usually gone only a few hours, but today was gone since morning.
The dog's hips are stiff and it tires quickly after excitement.
The dog spent the afternoon alone, pacing the fence line.
The older dog outranks it and does not tolerate being barreled into.
The owner smells of somewhere unfamiliar, which unsettles the dog as much as it excites it.

does.verb: runs in circles and shoves its head into

could_also.verb: barks and holds back at a distance
grabs a stick and drops it at the owner's feet
rolls onto its back near the owner's feet

would_not.verb: ignores the owner and goes to the older dog first
would_not.why: the bond that pulls it is with the owner, not the other dog, no matter what rank says

would_not.verb: stays lying by the door
would_not.why: the whole day of being alone is exactly what it is reacting against

then: It will keep close to the owner's legs for the next hour, underfoot at every step, then collapse near the door once the excitement burns off and its hips ache.
why: The bond and the unusually long absence outweigh its stiffness and the older dog's rank; it spends what energy it has on greeting rather than caution, even though nothing practical comes of it.
turns_on: how long the owner was away

who: A grown son sitting with his dying father.
place: A small bedroom lit by one lamp, the last night before the father is expected to die.
present: the dying father, mostly unconscious
a sister asleep in a chair by the wall
a cup of water untouched on the table

factors.fact: He has not spent a night under this roof in years but came back for this.
His father sat with his own dying mother the same way, and the son knows it.
He has not slept properly in two days and his eyes keep closing.
That his father will wake once, alone, and no one will be there.
In this house it is said a dying person should never be left in an empty room.
There is nothing left to treat or fix; the sister already sent for who could be sent for.

does.verb: sits upright by the bed and keeps watch

could_also.verb: wakes his sister to share the watch
talks quietly to his father as if he can hear
steps out for air and comes straight back

would_not.verb: goes to sleep in the next room
would_not.why: the custom and his own fear of his father waking alone rule it out even though nothing he does can change the outcome

would_not.verb: leaves to fetch a healer again
would_not.why: he already knows there is nothing more medicine can do

then: He will nod off sitting up more than once before morning, jerking awake each time to check his father is still breathing, and will remember this night regardless of when the end actually comes.
why: Custom and the debt he feels for his own father's vigil years ago outweigh his exhaustion; the watch changes nothing about what happens to his father but everything about how the son can live with it after.
turns_on: whether someone else can share the watch

who: A woman who has managed her family's grain fields for many years.
place: The edge of a wheat field on the morning of the first cutting, before the rest of the harvesters arrive.
present: two farmhands waiting with scythes
a young girl carrying a jug of last year's beer
a crow watching from a fence post

factors.fact: Her mother always poured the first cup onto the ground before anyone ate from the new grain.
She does not believe pouring beer on dirt changes whether the crop is good or bad.
The farmhands watch her to see whether the custom still holds this year.
Her mother died over the winter and this is the first cutting without her.
The workers expect the small ritual before they start; skipping it would unsettle them.

does.verb: pours a cup of beer onto the ground before the first stalks are cut

could_also.verb: says a few words about her mother before pouring
has the young girl pour it instead
pours a smaller amount than usual

would_not.verb: skips the pour and starts cutting straight away
would_not.why: knowing it does nothing for the crop is not the same as being willing to be the one who lets the custom die, especially this year

would_not.verb: gives a long speech about her mother
would_not.why: the workers are waiting to cut grain, not to hear grief

then: The farmhands will start cutting the moment the cup is empty, and by midday no one will mention it again, though she will think of her mother every time she smells spilled beer for years after.
why: What she believes about beer and crops does not enter into it; what the workers expect and what she owes her mother's memory decide it, even though she can name no practical effect at all.
turns_on: whether her mother died this year

who: An elderly woman walking to the well.
place: A dirt path outside the village that forks around an old dead oak split by lightning years ago.
present: a neighbor boy walking the other fork with a bucket
two goats grazing near the oak
the split, blackened oak itself

factors.fact: It is widely said in this village that walking between the two halves of a lightning-split tree brings bad luck.
The shorter path runs directly between the two halves and saves several minutes.
She has believed this since childhood and cannot make herself stop believing it.
Her knees ache badly today and the longer path means more walking.
The neighbor boy took the short path without a second thought.

could_also.verb: stops and mutters a small charm before crossing between the halves anyway
asks the boy to fetch her water instead
waits for someone else to pass through the oak first

would_not.verb: walks straight between the two halves like the boy did
would_not.why: knowing the boy suffered nothing does not undo decades of believing the tree is unlucky for her specifically

would_not.verb: turns back without fetching water at all
would_not.why: the fear is of the tree, not of the errand, so she still goes, just the long way

then: She will arrive at the well later and with sorer knees than if she had cut through, and will say nothing to the boy about why she went the long way.
why: Her aching knees argue for the short route and the boy's example shows it costs nothing, but a lifetime of belief about the split tree outweighs both; she pays the practical cost to avoid a risk she cannot prove is real.
turns_on: whether the tree was ever struck by lightning

who: A young man known among his friends for taking risks.
place: A river bend below a tall rock ledge, on a hot afternoon with several people swimming below.
present: three friends swimming in the river
a young woman he is trying to impress, sitting on the bank
a shallow gravel bar just visible under the water near the far bank

factors.fact: He already boasted loudly that he would jump from the highest ledge.
He has jumped from this ledge before, though not this high a spot on it.
The young woman on the bank laughed when a friend suggested he wouldn't dare.
His arm still aches faintly from a fall the week before.
Nothing depends on the jump; there is no fish to catch and no crossing to make.
Backing down in front of this group would cost him standing he cares about.

does.verb: climbs to the highest ledge and jumps

could_also.verb: jumps from a lower, familiar ledge instead
climbs down and says he changed his mind
waits and jumps only after someone else goes first

would_not.verb: checks the water depth carefully before jumping
would_not.why: a careful check would slow him down and look like fear in front of the group he is performing for

would_not.verb: refuses outright
would_not.why: he already committed himself loudly enough that backing out costs more standing than the jump risks

then: He will surface to laughing and cheering, milk the moment by swimming slowly to the bank, and privately be relieved the gravel bar was further out than it looked.
why: The boast already made and the audience watching outweigh the sore arm and the plain fact that nothing is gained by jumping; the display is the whole point.
turns_on: whether he already boasted he would jump

place: A kitchen after supper, right after being told he cannot have a second sweet cake.
present: his mother, still clearing the table
a younger sister eating her own cake without complaint
the empty plate where the cakes were

factors.fact: He is not actually hungry; he ate a full supper.
He was told plainly that there are no more cakes for tonight, not that he did something wrong.
His sister got a cake earlier just like he did, so nothing was unfair.
He is tired from a long day and small refusals hit harder than usual when he is tired.
Complaining loudly has occasionally gotten him an extra treat before, though not tonight.

does.verb: crosses his arms and refuses to answer

could_also.verb: stomps off to another room without a word
complains loudly that it isn't fair
pokes at his sister's cake out of spite

would_not.verb: asks calmly for a cake tomorrow instead
would_not.why: he is too tired and too caught up in the moment to reason his way to a sensible request

would_not.verb: cries loudly
would_not.why: the refusal was mild enough that outright crying would feel, even to him, like too much

then: He will sit with his arms crossed for several minutes, ignored by everyone, and eventually wander off to play as if nothing happened, with no cake gained by any of it.
why: Tiredness turns a small, fair refusal into something that feels bigger than it is; sulking gets him nothing but is the only response his mood leaves room for, since the refusal itself was too mild to justify a bigger fuss.

who: A young woman and her older brother.
place: A shed at the back of their house where they are sorting old tools together.
present: a large spider in a web in the corner of the shed
a box of rusted tools between them

factors.fact: She jumped and yelped loudly the moment she saw the spider.
They tease each other often and neither takes it badly, most of the time.
He knows exactly how much it will bother her if he brings it closer.
As the older brother he has teased her about this same fear since they were children.
She helped him with a chore yesterday without complaint.

does.verb: picks up a stick and pretends to nudge the spider toward

could_also.verb: kills the spider without comment
tells her calmly there's a spider and to move away
ignores the spider and keeps sorting tools

would_not.verb: actually flicks the spider onto her
would_not.why: the teasing has a line, and crossing from pretend to real would turn a joke into something she wouldn't forgive

would_not.verb: apologizes for startling her
would_not.why: the yelp is exactly the reaction that makes the teasing worth doing, not something he regrets causing

then: She will swat at him and call him an idiot, he will laugh, and within a minute they will be back to sorting tools as if nothing happened.
why: Their easy bond and his knowledge of exactly what unsettles her make the tease worth doing for no gain but her reaction; the debt from yesterday's help doesn't weigh against it since neither of them treats the teasing as unkind.
turns_on: whether she reacted visibly to the spider

place: His neighbor's yard, just after the neighbor's old milking goat died overnight.
present: the neighbor, crying quietly beside the dead goat
the goat's body, already stiff
two of the neighbor's children standing back, unsure what to do

factors.fact: He and the neighbor have helped each other for years.
There is nothing to be done for the goat; it is already dead.
The goat was old and the neighbor's main source of milk, but the crying is plainly about more than the milk.
He was on his way to his own morning chores when he saw the neighbor outside.
The neighbor is not a person who normally shows tears in front of others.

does.verb: sits down beside him without saying much

could_also.verb: offers to help bury the goat
offers milk from his own goats until the neighbor can get another
sends the children inside and stays with the neighbor alone

would_not.verb: points out that the goat was old and would have died soon anyway
would_not.why: it is true and it is exactly the kind of true thing that helps no one crying

would_not.verb: leaves quickly to get to his own chores
would_not.why: the bond between them means the sight of a crying neighbor pulls harder than an unfinished chore that can wait

then: He will stay a while longer than he meant to, help move the goat's body later that morning, and be late to his own chores without minding much.
why: Nothing he does brings the goat back or changes the neighbor's morning, but the bond between them and the plain fact of a grown man crying outweigh the pull of his own waiting chores.
turns_on: how long he was already planning to stay

who: Two boys, around twelve years old.
place: A field at the edge of the village where a wild, unfamiliar-looking mushroom is growing at the base of a stump.
present: the mushroom itself, pale and unfamiliar
a group of three other children watching

factors.fact: One boy just claimed the other is too afraid to eat anything strange.
He does not actually know whether the mushroom is safe to eat.
Losing the dare in front of the watching children would mark him as the timid one for weeks.
He has heard stories of people made sick by wild mushrooms.
He could touch it or smell it without eating it and still seem brave enough.

does.verb: breaks off a small piece and pretends to consider eating it, then throws it at

could_also.verb: actually bites into the mushroom
refuses the dare outright
dares him back to eat it first

would_not.verb: eats the whole mushroom without hesitation
would_not.why: the fear of being made sick is real enough that even wanting to win, he looks for a way out of actually swallowing it

would_not.verb: walks away without responding to the dare
would_not.why: walking away in front of the watching children would cost him exactly the standing the dare threatens

then: The other children will laugh either way, the dare will be half-forgotten by evening, and neither boy will actually be sick from it.
why: His fear of the unknown mushroom is stronger than his fear of being called timid, so he finds a way to look bold without swallowing anything; nothing is gained by any version of it, which is rather the point of a dare.
turns_on: whether he knows the mushroom is safe

who: A prosperous farmer attending a neighbor's daughter's wedding.
place: The yard of the neighbor's house, set up with tables for a wedding feast.
present: the bride and groom
the bride's father, a farmer of modest means
other guests, several bringing smaller, ordinary gifts

factors.fact: He is known as the wealthiest farmer in the area and is expected to act like it.
The bride's father once lent him a plow horse for a season without asking anything back.
Another wealthy guest already gave a modest, ordinary gift, leaving room to be noticed.
Wedding gifts are usually practical: tools, cloth, a young animal.
He wants it said around the village that he gave the finest gift anyone had seen at a wedding here.

does.verb: presents a young ox, far beyond what the occasion calls for

could_also.verb: gives a generous but ordinary gift like the other guests
gives the ox privately to the father instead of announcing it at the feast
gives nothing beyond a kind word, citing the debt already repaid

would_not.verb: gives the ox without any announcement or ceremony
would_not.why: an unannounced gift does nothing for what he wants known around the village, which is most of his reason for giving it

would_not.verb: gives a gift smaller than what other wealthy guests gave
would_not.why: his rank and his wish to be talked about rule out anything that would not stand out

then: The gift will be the talk of the wedding and of the village for weeks, the bride's father will feel obligated in a way that outweighs the old debt, and the young couple will have an ox they now must feed and house.
why: The debt he owes the father would be repaid by any decent gift, but his rank and his wish to be seen as the finest giver push him toward something far past what is owed or needed; the gift serves his name more than the couple.
turns_on: whether another wealthy guest already gave a modest gift

who: A rooster kept with a small flock of hens.
place: A farmyard in the early morning, with the hens scattered nearby feeding.
present: several hens pecking at the ground
a second, younger rooster kept in a separate pen nearby
a dog dozing in the shade, uninterested

factors.fact: It molted recently and its tail feathers have only just grown back full.
It is the only rooster loose among these hens; the younger one is penned separately.
It is not hungry and there is no food to lead the hens to.
One particular hen wandered close to it a moment ago.
Nothing nearby threatens it; the dog is dozing and pays it no attention.

could_also.verb: crows loudly instead
scratches at the ground and calls the hens over as if it found food
postures at the younger rooster's pen fence out of habit

would_not.verb: attacks the hen
would_not.why: the display is not aggression and nothing about the hen's approach calls for driving her off

would_not.verb: ignores the hen entirely
would_not.why: a hen wandering close with fresh tail feathers to show off is exactly the moment the display exists for

then: The hen may wander off within a minute regardless, and the rooster will go back to ordinary pecking, having gained nothing but having done what it does.
why: Freshly regrown feathers and a hen nearby set off the strut on their own, without hunger or threat driving it; the display is not aimed at food or safety, only at being seen.
turns_on: whether its tail feathers have grown back

who: A working horse pulling a small cart.
place: A narrow wooden bridge over a shallow stream that the horse has crossed many times before.
present: the driver holding the reins
the cart loaded with sacks of grain
the stream running low and calm beneath the bridge

factors.fact: It crossed this same bridge without trouble two days ago.
Nothing about the bridge looks different: no new gap, no loose board that either of them can see.
Something about the light or the shadow on the boards today unsettles it in a way neither horse nor driver can name.
The driver is firm with the horse and has never let a refusal stand before.
The grain needs to reach the mill by midday or the trip is wasted.

does.verb: plants its feet and refuses to step onto

could_also.verb: backs up several steps and tries to turn around
steps on after being led across on foot first
crosses eventually after standing a long while

would_not.verb: bolts and runs off the road entirely
would_not.why: its fear is focused on the bridge itself, not on panic that would carry it past the driver's control

would_not.verb: crosses immediately once urged
would_not.why: whatever unsettles it about the boards today is stronger, for now, than its habit of obeying

then: After some minutes of coaxing and one failed attempt, the driver will lead it across on foot by the bridle, after which it crosses without further trouble and the grain reaches the mill late but intact.
why: Nothing visibly changed about the bridge to explain the refusal; some fear neither horse nor driver can name outweighs, for a while, both its own recent crossing and the driver's usual firmness.
turns_on: whether anything about the bridge visibly changed

place: A kitchen floor where a shallow pan of water sits catching a drip from the roof after rain.
present: the pan of still water
the cat's owner, sitting nearby mending cloth
a mouse hole in the wall, currently empty

factors.fact: It has already eaten and is not hungry.
It has hunted mice from that hole before and could watch it instead.
It brushed past the pan and saw its own reflection move in the water.
It has seen its reflection in water before and never caught anything from it.

does.verb: paws at the water and watches its own reflection scatter

could_also.verb: watches the mouse hole instead
drinks from the pan without reacting to the reflection
loses interest and walks away after one paw swipe

would_not.verb: stalks the reflection as if it were prey to catch
would_not.why: it has learned before that nothing comes of catching the shape in the water, so the fascination stays playful rather than a real hunt

would_not.verb: ignores the water entirely
would_not.why: a moving reflection right after it brushed past is too immediate a thing to simply not notice

then: It will paw at the water a few more times, scattering the reflection each time, before wandering off toward the mouse hole once the water stills and stops moving.
why: Nothing it wants, food or prey, is actually in the pan, and it already knows that from past encounters with its own reflection; the fascination runs on the movement itself, not on any need.
turns_on: whether the water was disturbed enough to move

place: A small graveside marker at the edge of the village, on the anniversary of her husband's death.
present: the grave marker
a basket with a few flowers and a small loaf of bread
no one else nearby at this hour

factors.fact: She was married to him for over forty years.
She knows plainly that he cannot hear her.
It is the anniversary of his death, a day she has marked the same way every year since.
She has news, a grandchild born this year, that she would have told him first of anyone.
The walk to the grave is getting harder on her each year.

does.verb: sits by the marker and tells him about the new grandchild

could_also.verb: leaves the bread and flowers without speaking
asks a passing neighbor to walk her there next year instead
stays only a moment and leaves quickly

would_not.verb: stops visiting because he cannot hear her
would_not.why: knowing he cannot hear has never been the reason she comes, so it is not a reason to stop

would_not.verb: tells the news to a neighbor instead of coming to the grave
would_not.why: the news feels owed to him specifically, whether or not he can receive it

then: She will sit until her knees complain too much to stay longer, leave the bread and flowers as she always does, and walk home slower than she came.
why: What she knows about the dead not hearing does not outweigh forty years of habit and a need to tell him news she considers his by right; the harder walk each year has not yet been enough to stop her.

place: A barn loft stacked with hay, during a break from chores while her mother works nearby.
present: her mother, sorting tools below in the barn
a ladder up to the loft
a cat asleep in the hay

factors.fact: There is no chore she is avoiding; her chores for the morning are already done.
Her mother called her name a moment ago, not urgently, just checking where she is.
She is small enough to fit behind the hay bales without being seen from the ladder.
She knows her mother will look for her and will not be truly worried for a long while yet.
She wants the moment of being found, not to actually go unnoticed.

does.verb: squeezes behind the hay bales and stays quiet

could_also.verb: answers her mother's call right away
hides somewhere more visible so she is found quickly
makes a small noise on purpose to be found sooner

would_not.verb: hides somewhere her mother would never think to check
would_not.why: the fun is in being found, so a hiding place too good would ruin the point of hiding at all

would_not.verb: stays hidden after her mother sounds worried
would_not.why: the bond and her sense of her mother's mood matter more to her than winning the game

then: Her mother will call again, climb partway up the ladder, and find her within a few minutes, at which point she will jump out laughing rather than staying hidden any longer.
why: With no chore to avoid and full trust that her mother isn't truly worried yet, the pull is toward the small thrill of being sought and found, not toward actually disappearing; that is also why she picks a hiding place easy enough to find her in time.
